summary: Specifies how to send IPv4 datagrams over an ATM data link, both in a default way and when flow labels are used with the Ipsilon Flow Management Protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to pack internet packets into the small cells that a special fast network uses, with an optional shortcut for conversations that last a while.

subtitle: How to send labeled IPv4 packets over ATM links.

tldr.problem: ATM is a fast network technology that uses small cells and virtual circuits, while IPv4 uses datagrams. They have different packet structures, so IPv4 must be encapsulated when sent over ATM. When IFMP labels are used, the encapsulation changes based on the flow type.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1954 specifies three encapsulation methods for IPv4 on ATM: a default encapsulation using LLC/SNAP, and two optimized encapsulations for labeled flows that omit redundant header fields depending on the flow type.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 packets can be efficiently transmitted over ATM, with or without IFMP labels. The labeled encapsulations reduce overhead by removing header fields that are redundant or already captured in the IFMP flow identifier.

facts.label: Label format
facts.value: 32-bit (4 reserved bits, 12 VPI bits, 16 VCI bits)

today: RFC 1954 is an Informational document specifying Ipsilon Networks' protocol for IPv4 transmission over ATM with flow labels. It has not been adopted as a standards track specification and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies how to transmit IPv4 datagrams over an ATM data link in two scenarios: in the default case without labels, and when flow labels are applied via the Ipsilon Flow Management Protocol (IFMP, described in RFC 1953).

ATM is a connection-oriented network technology where data is sent in small fixed-size cells over virtual circuits identified by VPI (Virtual Path Identifier) and VCI (Virtual Circuit Identifier) pairs. The default encapsulation uses LLC/SNAP headers and is always available. When IFMP is used to label flows, optimized encapsulations can omit certain redundant IPv4 header fields to reduce overhead.

The document defines the label format for ATM and three flow-specific encapsulations corresponding to the three flow types defined in RFC 1953.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM is like a fast express postal system with many sorting bins. This RFC explains how to wrap internet packets so they fit properly in ATM's bins and how to handle shortcuts for regular mail runs.

sections.title: Labels on ATM
sections.content:
In IFMP, a label is a 32-bit value. On ATM, labels are mapped to VPI/VCI pairs: the low 16 bits of the label correspond to the VCI, and the next 12 bits correspond to the VPI. The high 4 bits are reserved and must be set to zero.

If a link cannot support the full 12-bit VPI or 16-bit VCI, the unused bits must be the most significant bits and must be set to zero.

The label space is managed at each end of a link, and each label maps to a virtual circuit on that link.
sections.plainLanguage: A label is just a pair of numbers that pick which bin and which slot within that bin to use on the ATM network.

sections.title: Default Encapsulation
sections.content:
The default encapsulation for IPv4 on ATM is the LLC/SNAP encapsulation specified in RFC 1483. Every IPv4 packet is prefixed with an 8-byte LLC/SNAP header (bytes 0xAA 0xAA 0x03 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x08 0x00) that identifies the protocol as IPv4.

The entire packet (header plus IPv4 datagram) is then encapsulated within the payload of an AAL-5 CPCS-PDU (ATM Adaptation Layer 5 Common Part Convergence Sublayer Protocol Data Unit). AAL-5 adds padding (0 to 47 octets) and an 8-octet trailer.

The maximum transmission unit (MTU) for IPv4 datagrams using the default encapsulation is 1500 octets. Default encapsulation frames are sent to VPI = 0, VCI = 15.

IFMP protocol messages must use the default encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The default way is to add a label and an envelope to the internet packet, like putting a certified letter in a box. The biggest letter is 1500 bytes.

sections.title: Flow Type 0: Changing Encapsulation
sections.content:
Flow Type 0 uses null encapsulation: the IPv4 datagram is placed directly in the AAL-5 payload with no LLC/SNAP header. This encapsulation is used when redirecting all IPv4 traffic, without regard to source or destination.

Because Flow Type 0 matches all IPv4 packets (regardless of source, destination, port, or other fields), it offers a simple way to apply a label to general IPv4 traffic.

The MTU is 1500 octets, and frames are sent to the VPI/VCI specified in the IFMP Flow Type 0 Redirect message.
sections.plainLanguage: Flow Type 0 is the simplest: just put the internet packet directly in the envelope, without the certified mail label, for very general traffic.

sections.title: Flow Types 1 and 2: Optimized Encapsulations
sections.content:
Flow Type 1 uses null encapsulation and omits several redundant IPv4 header fields: Version, IHL, Type of Service, TTL, Protocol, and both addresses. It also omits the first 4 octets after the IP header (the source and destination ports for TCP and UDP). The MTU is reduced to 1484 octets (1500 minus 16 bytes).

Flow Type 2 is similar but keeps the source and destination ports and omits only Version, IHL, TTL, and the addresses. Its MTU is 1492 octets (1500 minus 8 bytes).

Both use the checksum value that would result if the TTL field were zero. This allows the receiver to verify the checksum even though the TTL may differ.

These optimized encapsulations reduce overhead for labeled flows by removing header information that is already known from the IFMP flow identifier (which includes addresses and ports for both Type 1 and Type 2).
sections.plainLanguage: For regular conversations, we can skip writing down the address and some other stuff because both routers already know it from the label. This saves space in the envelope.
